issue.issue_text: Whether Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) is applicable when there are five or more accused persons named in the FIR, even if their trials are separated.

facts: Five accused persons were specifically named in the First Information Report (FIR).
Initially, the investigating officer filed a charge-sheet against only two of the accused.
The remaining three accused were added later by the trial court under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
Because these three accused absconded, their trial was separated from the others.
The High Court had ruled that Section 149 IPC was not applicable because the initial charge-sheet was against only two people and the others were being tried separately.
law: Section 149 of the IPC makes every member of an unlawful assembly guilty of an offence committed by any other member in pursuit of the assembly's common object.
An "unlawful assembly" under Section 141 IPC requires five or more persons.
The essential question for applying Section 149 is whether an unlawful assembly of five or more persons existed at the time of the offence.

The identity of all persons in the assembly is a matter for determining individual guilt. A conviction with the aid of Section 149 is possible even if fewer than five persons are convicted, as long as the court is satisfied that the convicted individuals were part of a larger assembly of five or more, who may be known or unknown, identified or unidentified.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had "seriously erred" by focusing on the number of people in the initial charge-sheet and the fact that the trials were separated.
The Court held that the crucial factor was that five persons were named in the FIR and all five were facing trial for the crime, even if their trials were separate.
The separation of trials does not change the fundamental allegation that an unlawful assembly of five people was formed to commit the offence.
The Court reasoned that the existence of an unlawful assembly is the primary condition. Since five people were named and were being prosecuted, the requirement for Section 149 was met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that Section 149 of the IPC is applicable. The Court held that as long as five or more persons are alleged to have formed an unlawful assembly and are facing trial for the offence, Section 149 can be invoked, regardless of whether they were all included in the initial charge-sheet or if their trials were subsequently separated.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in acquitting the accused for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC.

facts: The trial court convicted the respondent-accused for murder under Section 302 with the aid of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
On appeal, the High Court set aside this conviction. It acquitted the accused of the murder charge but convicted him for the lesser offense under Section 323 IPC (voluntarily causing hurt).

The High Court's reasoning was that Section 149 IPC was not applicable because the initial charge-sheet was filed against only two accused persons. Three other individuals were added later and were being tried separately.
The original complainant appealed the High Court's acquittal to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 149 of the IPC establishes vicarious liability for members of an unlawful assembly. It states that if an offense is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in pursuit of a common object, every person who was a member of that assembly is guilty of that offense.
For Section 149 to apply, there must be an unlawful assembly, which requires a minimum of five persons.
A member of an unlawful assembly can be held liable for the specific acts of another member, including a fatal blow, if they shared the common object.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's reasoning was flawed and that it had "seriously erred" in its conclusion.
The Court noted that five persons were specifically named in the First Information Report (FIR) from the beginning.
The fact that three of these accused were charge-sheeted later and were being tried separately did not negate the existence of an unlawful assembly or the applicability of Section 149 IPC.
The Court held that since the respondent was found to be a member of the unlawful assembly and had participated in the crime, he was vicariously liable for the murder.
Therefore, even though another accused delivered the fatal blow, the respondent was equally guilty of murder under Section 302 with the aid of Section 149 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in acquitting the accused. It held that Section 149 IPC was clearly applicable as there were five accused named in the FIR who formed an unlawful assembly. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed the High Court's judgment, restored the trial court's conviction for murder, and sentenced the accused to life imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the contention that the injury on the neck was not established and proved is a valid ground for acquittal.

facts: The accused contended that the injury on the deceased's neck had not been established and proved.
The court noted that the depositions of eyewitnesses (PW1 and PW4) and the doctor (PW7) were relevant evidence against the accused.
The medical evidence described injury no. 9 as a "6xl.5 cm blue colored wound on the back of neck" with broken fourth and fifth cervical ribs.
According to the doctor's deposition and medical opinion, the cause of death was specifically injury no. 9, resulting from the "shock of wound at spinal bone of neck."
application: The Court directly addressed the accused's submission by examining the evidence on record.
It relied on the combined testimony of the eyewitnesses and the medical evidence provided by the doctor (PW7).

The Court found that the doctor's opinion and deposition explicitly established not only the existence of the neck injury (injury no. 9) but also that it was the fatal blow leading to the victim's death.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that the neck injury was not established. It held that the medical evidence, including the doctor's deposition and the detailed description of injury no. 9, along with eyewitness testimony, conclusively proved the existence and fatal nature of the neck wound.

issue.issue_text: Whether the accused ought to have been convicted for the offence under Section 323 IPC.

facts: The High Court had set aside the accused's conviction for murder (Section 302/149 IPC) and instead convicted him for the lesser offence of voluntarily causing hurt (Section 323 IPC).

The High Court's reasoning was that after removing the charge of unlawful assembly (Section 149 IPC), it had to consider the accused's individual act, which, given the weapon (lathi) and the fact another person delivered the fatal blow, only amounted to an offence under Section 323 IPC.
Although the accused had not formally appealed his conviction under Section 323 IPC, the Supreme Court heard his counsel's arguments on the merits of this conviction.
application: The Supreme Court's primary analysis focused on whether the High Court was correct to acquit the accused of the more serious charge under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC.
The Court found that the High Court had "seriously erred" in holding that Section 149 IPC (unlawful assembly) was not applicable.

The Supreme Court concluded that the accused, being part of the unlawful assembly, was liable for the murder committed by another member (Bhupendra Singh) under Section 302 with the aid of Section 149 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court's decision was to quash and set aside the High Court's judgment. By restoring the more serious conviction for murder under Section 302/149 IPC, the court implicitly upheld that the accused was, at a minimum, guilty of the lesser offence under Section 323 IPC. The court did not acquit the accused of the Section 323 charge after hearing arguments, instead finding him guilty of a graver crime that encompassed the act of causing hurt.

cases.case_name: Bharwad Mepa Dana & Anr. Vs. State of Bombay
cases.principle: For the application of Section 149 IPC, establishing that an unlawful assembly consisted of five or more persons is sufficient, even if they are tried separately.

cases.principle: For the distinction between the first part and the second part of Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A court errs in law when it concludes that no case is made out to invoke Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) if the facts and circumstances of the case sufficiently establish the existence of an unlawful assembly and a common object.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court has seriously erred in observing that no case is made out to invoke Section 149 IPC. Under the circumstances the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court acquitting the accused for the offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC is unsustainable and the same deserves to be quashed and set aside.
legal_tests_applied: Heavy reliance is placed on the decision of this Court in the case of Bharwad Mepa Dana & Anr. Vs. State of Bombay 1960 (2) SCR 172 as well as Mizaji and Anr. Vs. The State of U.P. (1959) Supp. (1) SCR940.
